name: Domaine Pierre Usseglio & Fils Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2015
text:
## Domaine Pierre Usseglio & Fils Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2015

**The story.** Domaine Pierre Usseglio & Fils is an immigrant's success story. Francis Usseglio came to the Rhône from Italy in 1931, one of the many [Italians who settled in France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italians_in_France), and founded the domaine in [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC) in 1948. He had two sons, Pierre and Raymond. Pierre took over the family estate, while Raymond started his own winery in 1960, which is why there are two different Usseglio estates in the village today. Since 1999 Pierre's sons, Jean-Pierre and Thierry, have run Domaine Pierre Usseglio, and a new generation, Gregory Usseglio, now works there full-time ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

The estate has 24 hectares spread over 17 small parcels across the appellation, on a mix of sand, clay, limestone and stones. The vineyards are about 80% [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), 10% [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah), 5% [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre) and 5% [Cinsault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinsaut); the family pulled out its [Counoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counoise) and [Muscardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscardin) and replanted Grenache ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The wine: the classic Châteauneuf.** This is the estate's classic Châteauneuf, its main red, often sold as the "Tradition". It is a classic blend of about 75 to 80% [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), with [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah), [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre) and a splash of [Cinsault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinsaut). Jeb Dunnuck calls it a "rock star traditional cuvée". For 2015 Jeff Leve gives 80% Grenache, 10% Syrah, 5% Cinsault and 5% Mourvèdre ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) says Grenache suffered from [coulure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coulure) at flowering in 2015, so yields were lower but quality very promising, with higher alcohol than in the two previous years; she doesn't expect the 2015s to live as long as the 2016s.

**What the critics say for 2015.**
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 91** (August 2017). "Soft, polished and silky with sweet, red fruits, thyme and spice"; forward in style and "already quite fun to drink".
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 91.0** (from your CellarTracker list).
- (I couldn't read other critics' notes for the 2015 classic cuvée, so I've left them out.)

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is eleven years old. A forward wine from a vintage Jancis Robinson doesn't expect to be as long-lived as 2016, so drink it over the next few years: red fruit, thyme, spice and earth. Decant gently.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, for freshness and lift. Young bottles do well with 1 to 2 hours in a [decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation); older ones need only enough to leave the sediment behind. It says the estate's wines are usually best with 3 to 5 years in bottle, and the best vintages drink well from 5 to 18 years after the harvest ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, sausages, grilled meats, barbecue and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), as well as tuna, salmon, mushrooms, eggplant and tomatoes. For an all-Grenache wine like this, with its raspberry and kirsch fruit, my picks are a slow-roasted lamb shoulder with garlic and thyme, duck breast with a cherry sauce, a Provençal [ratatouille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratatouille) or a [porcini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boletus_edulis) risotto. I'd avoid very spicy food, which makes the alcohol feel hotter.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists this wine at the moment.

**From the history books**
- **The popes and their castle.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V) moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards to the north and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules in 1923, made law in 1936 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). The Grenache for Mon Aïeul was planted in 1926, right in the middle of that story.
- **From Italy, 1931.** Francis Usseglio arrived from Italy in 1931 and founded his own domaine in 1948, three years after the end of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II) ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **A fiftieth birthday.** In 1999 the family released a one-off Cuvée de Cinquantenaire, 200 cases of old-vine Grenache, ("cinquantenaire" means fiftieth anniversary). It became the forerunner of the Réserve des Deux Frères ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Curious details**
- **"Not For You".** The brothers have made a wine called "Not For You" only twice, in 2007 and 2016, from Grenache close to 100 years old in Les Grandes Serres. It took almost two years to finish fermenting and reached close to 18% alcohol. Fewer than 400 bottles were made ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **Bottles too big for the rack.** The sister wine, Réserve des Deux Frères, comes in oversized bottles that don't fit standard wine racks, as Jeff Leve warns from experience.
- **Stems in the vat.** Since 2001 the Usseglios have fully destemmed the grapes for their other reds, but Mon Aïeul still goes into the vat as whole bunches, stems and all ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pierre-usseglio-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **Two Usseglio estates.** Domaine Pierre Usseglio and Domaine Raymond Usseglio are separate wineries, founded by Francis's two sons, so don't mix up the labels.
- **The famous stones.** Parcels such as [La Crau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=La+Crau,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) are covered in [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), smooth quartzite stones left by Alpine glaciers and rounded over millennia by the Rhône. They soak up the sun by day and give the heat back to the vines at night, and in dry summers they help keep moisture in the soil ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954, after local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), the Châteauneuf council banned "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. The decree is still in force, and a Californian Rhône-style wine from [Bonny Doon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonny_Doon_Vineyard), Le Cigare Volant, is named after the tale ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
